system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2137-08-30 21:37:00 to 2137-08-31 19:18:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for progressive dyspnea and productive cough over three weeks, consistent with mucus accumulation due to recurrent tracheal stenosis from relapsing polychondritis and SMAD4 syndrome. He had missed a scheduled bronchoscopy and presented with increased yellow tracheal secretions. He underwent flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of the trachea and both main bronchi, which relieved his symptoms. Bronchial washings grew Klebsiella oxytoca, prompting a seven-day course of cefpodoxime. A CT chest showed stable airway stenosis and no acute findings despite transient desaturation with ambulation. His white blood cell count improved from 14.0 to 10.7, and he was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to complete antibiotics, continue baseline medications, and follow up with interventional pulmonology and primary care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You're here tonight for your scheduled bronchoscopy with balloon dilation. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi doctor. I’m okay, a bit nervous. My breathing’s been a little worse since last time, but not bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your CT scan showed the trachea and bronchi are still narrowed from your polychondritis. The procedure tomorrow will help open them up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, like last time. I remember the dilation helped. But I’ve been seeing those lung spots on my scans—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new spots on your left lower lobe and right lung apex could be infection or inflammation. But you’re not running a fever or coughing more, so we don’t think it’s active. Infectious disease agrees—no antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But my white count is high again, right? It was 19.6 when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white count is elevated, mostly neutrophils. But since you’re not sick-appearing and cultures show colonizing bacteria like Pseudomonas and Klebsiella, we believe this is from chronic airway inflammation, not a new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the bacteria in my lungs are just… living there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’re colonizers—common in patients with tracheostomies and chronic airway disease. Treating them wouldn’t help and might cause resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about after the procedure? Will I be in pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might have some soreness around the trach site. We’ll give oxycodone and acetaminophen as needed. Most patients say it feels like usual post-dilation discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The bronchoscopy went well—no complications. They dilated your trachea and main bronchi. You had some mucosal inflammation, but that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My breathing feels about the same so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might take a day or two to notice improvement. We’ve started you on 50 mg of prednisone to reduce airway swelling, and you’ll taper it down over the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only on 2.5 mg before. Is such a high dose safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a short course. We’re using it to calm the inflammation after the procedure. You’ll decrease by 10 mg every three days until you’re back to 7.5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving—white count dropped to 13.3. You’re saturating well on 40% oxygen. We’re comfortable sending you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on your breathing, fever, or increased secretions. Finish the prednisone taper, stay on your regular methotrexate and inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see interventional pulmonology and rheumatology soon. We’ll also repeat a CBC to monitor your white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Your breathing sounds stable, and your trach site looks good—just a little redness, no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the prednisone as directed, use albuterol if short of breath, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my appointments lined up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The team will get your discharge papers ready.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for a scheduled bronchoscopy with balloon dilation due to recurrent tracheobronchial stenosis from relapsing polychondritis and Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome. The procedure was performed without complications, and he was observed post-operatively. His breathing remained stable, and pain was controlled with oxycodone. Elevated white blood cell count persisted but was attributed to chronic inflammation rather than active infection, supported by the absence of fever or increased secretions. He was started on a prednisone taper from 50 mg to his baseline 7.5 mg and discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned in pulmonology and rheumatology.
